defining_records.title: Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose: A Critical Edition — the Footnote to Pearl (Lee Sharks & Jack Feist, 2014), with Its Drafts, Witnesses, Intertexts and Operations, and Kerouac's List Item by Item (EA-BTP-EDITION-01 v1.1)

captures.q: What are the arguments in “Belief & Technique for Telepathic Prose: A Critical Edition” by Lee Sharks (Alexanarch deposit #1717, AXN:0AA0)? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.
captures.description: THE CRITICAL EDITION (#1717) ON CHATGPT, SIGNED OUT, AT THE QUESTION ITS RECORD PAGE'S LINK SENDS: the answer reads the full text and reports it closely. It gives the six measures of §8.2 by name and in order, the copy-text's 24 items against the blog's 23 numerals with the author's ruling on items 20 and 21, the operations of collision, literalization, enactment, repetition, recursion and sublation, the readings of items 12, 15, 23 and 24, Dickinson's letter of 7 June 1862, and the edition's limit on its own comparison (item against item; corpus against corpus the comparison is not made). It opens by setting the poem in parody, 'the piece does not merely parody writing advice', and calls the telepathic premise 'a self-referential joke'; the operator's ruling makes the piece a deeply serious ars poetica that contains the parodic among almost every other genre. It never names the occasion the edition states first, the machine readers that file the piece under Kerouac, nor the originals library, the Capture Registry, the licence, or Jack Feist as a heteronym.

inversions.against: the operator's ruling of 2026-10-29, carried in the poem's set and in #1716: the piece is 'a deeply serious ars poetica that contains and enacts' the comic, the parodic and the satirical 'among almost every other genre' and 'is not a comic, parodic, or satirical ars poetica'. The answer grants the parody as the base and adds to it; it repeats the frame for item 12 ('more than a joke'), item 18 ('The joke'), the title ('not merely a comic substitution') and item 1 ('a self-referential joke'). The edition's evaluative claim itself (item against item, corpus against corpus not made) is reported at its force.
